description: Trampolines were designed as training equipment for adults. How children get hurt on trampolines, typical injuries, and legal issues in injury claims.
shortAnswer: The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has repeatedly warned parents and anyone else who cares about child safety to keep kids off trampolines. Emergency Departments across the country see nearly 100,000 injuries from trampolines each year. It's not just at jump parks that kids get hurt; it's at homes also.

faq.q: How do children typically get hurt on trampolines?
faq.a: Typical ways include too many children on the trampoline, falls from the trampoline, impact with the trampoline frame or springs, colliding with other children in mid air, and somersaults/flips. Approximately 3/4 of trampoline injuries occur when multiple people were using the trampoline.

faq.q: What are the most common and most serious trampoline injuries in children?
faq.a: Ankle injuries are the most common form of injury children sustain while jumping on a trampoline. Head and neck injuries are the most serious child injuries typically seen resulting from trampoline accidents.

faq.q: Does homeowner's insurance cover a child's trampoline injury?
faq.a: Some homeowner's insurance companies exclude trampoline injuries from coverage, because trampolines are viewed as an "attractive nuisance." Homeowners who own trampolines may have to obtain a "rider" that expressly provides coverage for trampoline related claims.

faq.q: Can the assumption of the risk defense defeat a young child's trampoline injury claim?
faq.a: The efficacy of the "assumption of the risk" defense is close to nil with younger children, due to another legal doctrine, known as the "tender years doctrine." This doctrine holds that children under a certain age (probably 7) can not be charged with contributory negligence (fault) or assumption of the risk.
